citations.quote: For dependent deductions, the adopted premise is that on a finite fixed-endpoint timelike segment in a local potential domain, the model trajectory is stationary for the displayed action. The potential and metric are fixed inputs, $m>0$ and $q$ are constant, and this premise asserts neither a global potential nor global trajectory existence.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Use the smooth, time-oriented Lorentzian background $(M,g,N)$, signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and the distinct chart, observer, congruence, tetrad and worldline meanings of [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. The metric and time orientation are prescribed data, not dynamical variables. A **charged spinning test body** in this definition consists of the following model quantities along a massive worldline $z:I\to M$:

- $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval whose parameter is proper time $\tau$ in seconds; $z$ is $C^2$, future-directed and timelike, and $U:=dz/d\tau$ obeys $g(U,U)=-c^2$. The SI conversion constant is $c>0$ metres per second; in a flat specialization use the affine Minkowski model and the proper-time decomposition of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].
- The constant rest-mass parameter $m>0$ has unit kilogram, and the constant charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ has unit coulomb. They are primitive model parameters; this definition does not derive them from the background field or from another framework.
- The **kinetic four-momentum** is the derived vector $P:=mU$ along $z$, with unit kilogram metre per second. It is distinct from the potential-dependent covector defined in [[lem-rpm-charge-gauge-boundary]].
- The **spin or polarization vector** is a $C^1$ tangent vector field $s(\tau)\in T_{z(\tau)}M$ constrained by $g(s,U)=0$, so it lies in the positive-definite instantaneous rest space $U^\perp$. Its unit is angular momentum, kilogram metre squared per second. This is a classical model vector; no quantization or quantum spin state is defined here.
- The gyromagnetic ratio $g_s\in\mathbb R$ is a dimensionless primitive species parameter. In the instantaneous rest space the model defines the magnetic-moment vector by $\mu=(g_s q/2m)s$, with unit ampere metre squared. No value $g_s=2$ is assumed, and this constitutive relation is not deduced from Lorentz covariance or classical electromagnetism.
- The prescribed external electromagnetic field is a $C^1$ alternating covariant two-tensor $F$ on an open region of $M$, independent of the unknown curve. Define $F^\sharp:T M\to T M$ by $g(F^\sharp(v),w)=F(w,v)$. In the flat specialization, a named inertial chart with $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres uses $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, matching [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]. On the curved background, $F$ is only a two-form; at an event its components in a chosen orthonormal tetrad use the same algebraic convention. Such a tetrad is a basis field, not a coordinate chart or an observer congruence, as distinguished in [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. The components in an orthonormal tetrad have tesla units. This is an explicit curved-background model input. The cited EM supplier is a flat Minkowski definition and does not derive a curved field or curved Maxwell system.
- On any open potential domain where a $C^2$ covector field $A$ exists, $F=dA$ with components $F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a$ and $A$ has tesla metre components in the stated coordinates. No global potential is assumed, and no Maxwell equation or constitutive law is imposed here.

This is a test-body model on a fixed background: self-gravity, gravitational backreaction, self-field evaluation, radiation reaction, collisions, electric dipole moments, field-gradient translational forces and higher multipoles are outside this definition. Units follow the framework-local SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and do not identify quantities across frameworks.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure, as required for the metric-selected Levi–Civita connection $\nabla$ of [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Let $O\subseteq M$ be open and let $A$ be a $C^2$ covector field on $O$; define the $C^1$ two-form $F=dA$ by $F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a$ in each chart. Fix constants $c>0$, $m>0$ and $q\in\mathbb R$. Let $z:[a,b]\to O$ be a $C^2$ future-directed timelike curve, where $a<b$ are proper-time values in seconds and $U=dz/d\tau$ satisfies $g(U,U)=-c^2$. For every $C^2$ fixed-endpoint variation $z_\epsilon$ through timelike curves in $O$, with variation field $J=\partial_\epsilon z_\epsilon|_{\epsilon=0}$ and $J(a)=J(b)=0$, define

$$S[z_\epsilon]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(\partial_\tau z_\epsilon,\partial_\tau z_\epsilon)}\,d\tau+q\int_a^b A(\partial_\tau z_\epsilon)\,d\tau.$$

Then the first variation is

$$\delta S=\int_a^b\left[-m\,g(J,\nabla_UU)+qF(J,U)\right]d\tau.$$

Consequently, $z$ is stationary under all local chart-supported fixed-endpoint variations if and only if

$$m(\nabla_UU)_a=qF_{ab}U^b,$$

equivalently $m\nabla_UU=qF^\sharp(U)$, where $F^\sharp(v)$ is defined by $g(F^\sharp(v),w)=F(w,v)$. The statement is local to a potential domain; no global potential is assumed.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g(A) \subseteq B$, and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$. If $g$ is continuous
at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c) \in B$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ is continuous on $B$, then
$f \circ g$ is continuous on $A$.

**No side hypothesis is needed, and that is the whole point.** The composition
theorem for limits, [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]], must assume one of
two extra conditions: either $L \in B$ with $f(L) = M$, or $g \ne L$ on a
punctured neighbourhood of $c$; with both dropped the statement is false, which
is [[fs-naive-composition-of-limits]]. The first of those conditions is exactly
*continuity of $f$ at $L$* written out, so under the hypotheses above it holds
automatically and nothing has to be assumed. The mechanism is visible in the
proof: [[def-continuity-real]] quantifies over $|y - b| < \rho$ rather than over
$0 < |y - b| < \rho$, so the value $y = b$ that the limit version cannot control
is precisely the one the continuity hypothesis does control.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Let $I=[a,b]$ and $J=[\tilde a,\tilde b]$ be compact nondegenerate real intervals, let $\phi:J\to I$ be an admissible parameter change from [A1], and let $h:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. By [F5], $h$ is integrable. Define $H(x):=\int_a^x h(s)\,ds$; [F6] gives $H'=h$ on $I$, with one-sided derivatives at its endpoints. The chain rule [F3] applied to $G:=H\circ\phi$ gives $G'(\lambda)=h(\phi(\lambda))\phi'(\lambda)$ on $J$. This derivative is continuous by [F4] and therefore integrable by [F5]. Since $\phi(\tilde a)=a$ and $\phi(\tilde b)=b$, [F7] yields $\int_{\tilde a}^{\tilde b}h(\phi(\lambda))\phi'(\lambda)\,d\lambda=G(\tilde b)-G(\tilde a)=H(b)-H(a)=\int_a^b h(s)\,ds$. Thus the one-dimensional integral substitution used below holds for each continuous action integrand.

The segment in the statement is parameterized by proper time, and [A1] admits $\lambda=\tau$. If the same segment and variations are expressed in any other admissible parameter, step 2.1 proves that both the action and fixed-endpoint stationarity are unchanged. Therefore it suffices to test stationarity with $\lambda=\tau$. Under [A2], the curve, potential, regularity and endpoint hypotheses now match the local first-variation result [F2].

For any local fixed-endpoint variation $\gamma_\epsilon:[a,b]\to O$ from [A1], composition with $\phi$ gives a $C^2$ fixed-endpoint variation $\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi$ on $J$. In chart components, for $\widetilde\gamma^i(\epsilon,\lambda):=\gamma^i(\epsilon,\phi(\lambda))$, the first and second derivatives in $\lambda$ are $(\partial_s\gamma^i)\circ\phi\,\phi'$ and $(\partial_{ss}\gamma^i)\circ\phi\,(\phi')^2+(\partial_s\gamma^i)\circ\phi\,\phi''$; the derivatives in $\epsilon$ and the mixed derivative are $(\partial_\epsilon\gamma^i)\circ\phi$, $(\partial_{\epsilon\epsilon}\gamma^i)\circ\phi$ and $(\partial_{\epsilon s}\gamma^i)\circ\phi\,\phi'$. The chain and product rules [F3], together with continuity under composition and products [F4], show these derivatives are continuous, so the family remains $C^2$. Since $\phi'>0$, the composed curves remain future timelike and have the same endpoint events, and the chart-supported variation field remains supported in that chart. Bilinearity of $g$ gives $\sqrt{-g((\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi)',(\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi)')}=(\sqrt{-g(\gamma_\epsilon',\gamma_\epsilon')})\circ\phi\,\phi'$, and linearity of the covector $A$ gives $A((\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi)')=(A(\gamma_\epsilon'))\circ\phi\,\phi'$. Both scalar integrands are continuous by [F4]; applying step 1.1 to each proves $S[\gamma_\epsilon\circ\phi]=S[\gamma_\epsilon]$ for every $\epsilon$. Composition with $\phi^{-1}$ is the inverse map on variation families. Thus the action functions and their first variations agree, so stationarity is invariant under every admissible reparameterization.
derivations.rule: Transport the C2 fixed-endpoint variation family bijectively and apply the proved scalar substitution separately to both action integrands

derivations.claim: Applying [F2] under [A2], stationarity for every local fixed-endpoint variation is equivalent to $m(\nabla_UU)_a=qF_{ab}U^b$. Raising the covector index with the nondegenerate metric and using the definition of $F^\sharp$ in [F1] gives the equivalent vector equation $m\nabla_UU=qF^\sharp(U)$.

For a finite $C^2$ future-timelike curve segment $z:[a,b]\to O$ in that domain, where $a<b$ are proper-time endpoints, and the local $C^2$ fixed-endpoint variations of the postulate, choose the orientation-preserving parameter $\lambda=\tau$; the segment is stationary for the adopted action if and only if

Adopt as physical assumptions of the relativistic particle model, on top of the
flat spacetime model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and the SI unit
conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], together with
the framework's idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks and ideal light
signals:

**(i) Mass and momentum.** Every massive classical particle of the model
carries a positive constant invariant mass parameter $m>0$ and has
four-momentum $P=mU$, where $U$ is the four-velocity of its future timelike
worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]],
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]); $P$ is a vector of $V$
whose SI unit is kilogram metre per second. The formula is adopted only for
$m>0$; the case $m=0$ is not defined by it and is the separate premise
[[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]]. In particular $\eta(P,P)=-m^2c^2$
is a consequence of the four-velocity normalisation, not a separate
assumption.

**(ii) Observer measurement identification.** Relative to a future unit
observer $n$, the model identifies the measured energy of the particle with
$E_n(P)$, its measured spatial momentum with $q_n(P)$, its kinetic energy with
$T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ and its rest energy with $mc^2$, where $E_n,q_n,T_n$ are
the quantities of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]; the
units are the joule, kilogram metre per second and kilogram of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. This clause is a formulation
convention identifying mathematical quantities with the quantities the model
calls measured; it is not a measurement report and no experiment is claimed.

**(iii) Isolated collision balance.** An isolated collision is represented by
a mass-specified on-shell collision datum at an event, with finite nonempty
incoming and outgoing lists of the massive particles of (i) and/or the ideal
massless particles of [[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]], and with
no external four-momentum transfer or omitted leg. The interaction is
idealized as confined to that event. The sum of the incoming four-momenta equals the sum of the
outgoing four-momenta, in the sense of the collision data of
[[def-sr-collision-datum-and-conservation]]: the model adopts
$Q_{\mathrm{in}}=Q_{\mathrm{out}}$ for such an isolated datum. No particular
collision is asserted to occur, and no mechanism, probability, cross section
or amplitude is supplied by this clause.

**(iv) Equation of motion for a stipulated force.** Put
$H_c^+:=\{U\in C^+:\eta(U,U)=-c^2\}$. A stipulated force law is a given
map $F:D\to V$ on a given subset $D\subseteq A\times H_c^+$,
with force components in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2$. No regularity
away from the specified worldline is assumed. Along a given $C^2$ massive worldline
$x:I\to A$ with $(x(s),U(s))\in D$ for all $s\in I$, the model's particle
equation is $m\,dU/d\tau=F(x,U)$, with
$dU/d\tau$ the proper-time derivative of
[[def-sr-proper-time-derivative-and-four-force]], so that the stipulated $F$
is the four-force of the motion. A particular force law, and the existence,
uniqueness and domain of solutions of the resulting equation, are not adopted
here and belong to a separate model.

Empirical support for these assumptions is a nonlogical relation of the
framework, not a proof; the idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks,
ideal light signals and flat spacetime are inherited and travel to every
consumer of this premise.

Adopt as physical assumptions of this framework:

(i) The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ used by
[[def-em-lab-geometry]], together with the
conversion constant $c>0$ of [[def-em-si-conventions]], is the spacetime of the
framework: its points represent idealized physical events, displacements
represent idealized spacetime separations, and the causal classification of the
model is the framework's causal structure. In the concrete coordinate
realization [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]], $A=V=\mathbb R^4$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. That supplier uses the symbol $C^+$ for
the nonzero future causal cone, including null vectors; here, as in the
special-relativity model, $C^+$ denotes its future timelike subset. The
future null boundary vectors retain their separate causal classification.

(ii) The inertial frames and charts of
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] are the inertial descriptions of the
framework, and changes of description are the proper orthochronous isometries
adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]].

(iii) The ideal clock reading rule along future timelike curves and the
identification of ideal vacuum light rays with future null straight lines, both
with the same constant $c$, are those adopted in
[[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]].

(iv) The laboratory description of fields and sources is the restricted
inertial chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the spatial Euclidean structure
and the SI conventions of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

Status and scope: the mathematical model defines the geometry and its theorems
prove geometric facts only; that physical events are described by the model,
that ideal clocks read the stated proper time and that ideal vacuum light
follows null straight lines are adopted assumptions, not deductions from
experiment or from the mathematical axioms. The special-relativity postulates
adopted here do not by themselves select the Maxwell equations, a force law or
any matter model: the electromagnetic equations and couplings of this framework
are further postulates of it. The framework is classical, flat and non-quantum;
gravitational curvature, quantum fields and measurement postulates are outside
its scope.

Adopt as physical postulates of this framework, on the spacetime and particle
model of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] and on the special-relativity particle
model [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]:

(i) [Test charge in a prescribed external field] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a
constant charge parameter ([[def-em-sources]]), $m>0$ an externally supplied
rest mass, $x:J\to A$ a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline with
four-velocity $U$, and let $F$ be a prescribed field of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph
of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle. Adopt the equation of
motion

$$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),$$

where, at each original parameter $s\in J$, $\Phi=\Phi_{x(s)}$ is the
raised-index operator of the field at $x(s)$, defined by
$\eta(\Phi_{x(s)}(u),w)=F(x(s))(w,u)$
([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]); equivalently
$m\,dU^\mu/d\tau=q\,F^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$. Here $dU/d\tau$ is the derivative of $U$
with respect to its proper-time function $\tau(s)$: explicitly
$dU/d\tau=U'(s)/\tau'(s)$, with
$\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}>0$. It is the four-acceleration of the worldline
([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). The particle's own field
is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no
self-force.

(ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of
[[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated
matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density
$\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit
W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the
spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local
interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed
current alone.

(iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within
electromagnetism. The coupling is adopted for constant $q$ and $m>0$; no
magnetic-monopole coupling, no radiation reaction and no self-force are
included. In particular the nonrelativistic coordinate statement
$mr''=q(E+r'\times B)$ is not adopted as exact: the adopted statement is the
covariant one of clause (i), and any low-speed statement requires its own
approximation hypotheses and error bounds.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then
$e_i=+E_i/c$, $b_i=-B_i$ and $e_0=b_0=0$, and the invariants and square wedge
of that theorem read

$$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=+4\,(E\cdot B)/c,\qquad F\wedge F=-2\,(E\cdot B)\,\varepsilon/c,$$

where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are the spatial Euclidean structure of the frame.
(For the same pair $(E,B)$, that theorem's optional clause (d) uses
$F_{\rm optional}^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F_{\rm optional}^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, so
$F_{\rm optional}=-F$ in all six components, not only the magnetic block. This
framework fixes clause (a) and uses the theorem's general algebra; its optional
SI dictionary must be converted by negating the entire tensor.)

(c) [Potentials when they exist] If $\varphi$ and $A$ are $C^1$ with
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$A^\mu:=(\varphi/c,A)$, $A_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\nu}A^\nu$, then
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$; conversely, if a $C^1$
covector field $A_\mu$ on $U$ satisfies $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu
-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, then $E,B$ recovered from $F$ by clause (a) obey
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with
$\varphi:=-cA_0$ and the spatial potential vector $A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. Here
$\nabla$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] in the spatial coordinates,
and the spatial cross-product conventions of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] are
used. The definition does not assert that every field pair admits such a
potential; where a $C^1$ potential represents the $C^1$-or-better field of
clause (a), the field is closed in the explicit sense
$\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0$. This conclusion does not require second
classical derivatives of the potential: put
$H_{\lambda\mu\nu}:=\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}$, which is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$; for
every smooth compactly supported test $\psi$, substituting $F=dA$ and
integrating by parts twice, moving the derivatives first onto $\psi$
([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]] (b)) and then off the
potential factors after commuting only the smooth test derivatives
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]), gives $\int H\psi=0$; the
fundamental lemma (a) of [[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]
then gives $H=0$. The framework's potential theorems establish existence only
under their stated hypotheses; [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]
supplies the coordinate derivatives $\partial_\mu$ used throughout.

(d) [Four-current and index-raising operator] With the adopted four-current
$j=(c\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]], the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
[[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]], defined pointwise on $V$ by
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$, satisfies
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$; the components of $F$
carry the tesla (T), those of $j$ carry A m$^{-2}$, and those of a
four-potential $A^\mu$ carry T m.

The particle and light objects of the framework are the following curves and
vector fields of the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]],
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with the physical interpretation of
[[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and the units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Worldlines] A **worldline** is a regular causal curve $x:J\to A$ in one of
the regularity classes of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] ($J$ an
order-convex subset of $\mathbb R$ with at least two elements). A **massive
worldline** is a $C^k$ future timelike worldline, $k\ge1$, with everywhere
nonzero future timelike tangent. A **future null curve** is a $C^1$ curve with
everywhere nonzero future null tangent. An **ideal vacuum light ray** of the
adopted physical model follows a null straight line: on its parameter interval
it has the form $x(s)=p+\lambda(s)v$, where $p\in A$, $v\in V$ is nonzero
future null, and $\lambda$ is $C^1$ with $\lambda'(s)>0$. This is the
straight-ray adoption of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]]; arbitrary
future null curves are retained as kinematic objects without asserting that
they describe vacuum light propagation. Along a null curve the integrand
$-\eta(x',x')$ of the proper-time construction
([[def-sr-proper-time]]) vanishes identically, so that construction yields no
proper-time parametrization of it, and a light ray is never treated as a
massive worldline. A worldline is a curve in spacetime; its reading $r\circ x$
in a named laboratory chart is a coordinate description of it, not an object of
another observer.

(b) [Four-velocity and four-acceleration] For a massive worldline the
four-velocity $U$ and, when it is $C^2$, the four-acceleration $A$ are those of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]; wherever defined they satisfy
$\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$, by
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

(c) [Chart reading] If a massive $C^2$ worldline is described in a laboratory
chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] by $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ on an open interval of
laboratory times, then $|r'(t)|<c$ for every $t$, with four-velocity
$U=\gamma(c,r')$ and Lorentz factor
$\gamma=(1-|r'|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, by clause (e) of
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

(d) [Frames and observers] An inertial frame in this framework is the
origin-with-basis object of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]; a point
observer is a future unit timelike vector $n\in V$ with rest space $n^\perp$ and
rest projection $h$, as in clauses (c)-(d) of
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. On an open spacetime region
$W\subseteq A$, an **observer congruence field** means a $C^1$ map $n:W\to V$ with
$n(p)$ future timelike and $\eta(n(p),n(p))=-1$ at every $p$; its observer
histories, when given, are integral curves satisfying $dx/d\tau=cn(x)$.
A **tetrad field** is a tuple of $C^1$ maps $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3):W\to V^4$
whose values form a positively oriented $\eta$-orthonormal basis at every
event, with $f_0$ future timelike. Regularity here means componentwise $C^1$
in inertial coordinates. These fields need not be constant and are distinct
from an inertial origin-with-basis frame, its coordinate chart and a single
point observer; no global congruence or tetrad is asserted to exist.

(e) [Scope] No force law, no self-field and no extended-body structure is
supplied here; an accelerating massive worldline requires a force model stated
separately, and an ideal light ray carries no dispersive, quantum or
polarisation structure in this definition.

Assume the framework's spacetime, field and worldline objects of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]], with the SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and clause (i) of the adopted Lorentz coupling [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]]: a constant charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-sources]] (a), an externally supplied rest mass $m>0$, a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline $x:J\to A$ with four-velocity $U$, and a prescribed field $F$ of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle; the adopted equation of motion is $$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),\qquad \eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u),$$ $U$ the four-velocity of [[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] (b) with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$. Let $t\mapsto r(t)$ be the laboratory chart reading of the worldline, $v:=r'$ its coordinate velocity and $\gamma:=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, so that $U=\gamma(c,v)$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] (e)). Then, wherever the worldline is $C^2$: (a) [Coordinate force and power] with the coordinate three-momentum $p:=m\gamma v$ of [[pthm-sr-momentum-and-four-force]] (a), $$\frac{dp}{dt}=q\,(E+v\times B),\qquad \frac{d(\gamma mc^2)}{dt}=q\,E\cdot v,$$ the derivatives taken with respect to the chart time $t$ and $E,B$ the components of $F$ in the laboratory frame. (b) [Norm preservation] $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on $J$ with value $-c^2$; in particular a solution with future timelike initial data remains future timelike, and $|v(t)|<c$ wherever the reading is differentiable ([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]). (c) [Controlled low-speed expansion] for every $\delta\in(0,1)$, on any interval where $|v|/c\le\delta$, $$|\gamma-1|\le\frac{|v|^2/c^2}{2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},\qquad \Bigl|\gamma-1-\frac{|v|^2}{2c^2}\Bigr|\le\frac{3}{8}(1-\delta^2)^{-5/2}\Bigl(\frac{|v|^2}{c^2}\Bigr)^{2},$$ and consequently $$|p-mv|\le m|v|\,\frac{|v|^2}{2c^2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},\qquad \Bigl|\gamma mc^2-mc^2-\tfrac12m|v|^2\Bigr|\le\frac{3}{8}(1-\delta^2)^{-5/2}\frac{m|v|^4}{c^2};$$ the constants depend only on $\delta$, so the bounds are uniform in $|v|/c\le\delta$. These are pointwise algebraic expansions; they assert no approximation of the trajectory over a time interval, which would require a separate stability argument. (d) [Scope] The charge is constant, $m>0$ is an externally supplied parameter and $F$ is a prescribed exterior field: the particle's own field, radiation reaction and any self-force are excluded, as are magnetic monopoles and zero or variable mass; the nonrelativistic coordinate law is not adopted as exact, and (c) is a controlled kinematic expansion, not a trajectory approximation. The statement is conditional on the adopted postulates and makes no empirical claim.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, and let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^2$ future-timelike worldline in the flat Minkowski model of [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. Use one inertial frame and parameterize the curve by that chart's time coordinate $t$, so its coordinates are $(ct,\mathbf x(t))$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Identify the observer rest space with $\mathbb R^3$ by the frame's spatial orthonormal basis and use its Euclidean dot product and norm ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Write $\mathbf v=d\mathbf x/dt$, $\gamma=(1-|\mathbf v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, proper time $\tau$, and $U=dx/d\tau$. In the constant-mass sector of [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]], let $m>0$ be constant and $P=mU$. In this chart write $P=(E/c,\mathbf p)$, where $E$ and $\mathbf p$ are the observer energy and spatial momentum of [[def-rpm-mechanical-momentum-and-observer-energy]]. Then $|\mathbf v|<c$, $E=\gamma mc^2>0$, $\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v$, and

$$E^2=m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2,\qquad \mathbf v=\frac{c^2\mathbf p}{E}.$$

Define the three-force by $\mathbf F:=d\mathbf p/dt$ and the four-force by $K:=dP/d\tau$ in this flat inertial chart. In SI units $m$ is in kilograms, $c$ and $\mathbf v$ in metres per second, $E$ in joules, $\mathbf p$ in kilogram metres per second, and $\mathbf F,K$ in newtons. Then

$$\frac{dE}{dt}=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v,\qquad K=\gamma\left(\frac{\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v}{c},\mathbf F\right).$$

Separately, let $I_\tau\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open proper-time interval, let $m:I_\tau\to(0,\infty)$ be $C^1$, and let $U:I_\tau\to V$ be a $C^1$ future timelike vector field with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$. Measure $m$ in kilograms and $dm/d\tau$ in kilograms per second, and set $P(\tau):=m(\tau)U(\tau)$. With $K:=dP/d\tau$, the kinematic ansatz satisfies

$$\eta(P,K)=-m\,\frac{dm}{d\tau}\,c^2.$$

The last identity is only a differentiated mass-shell relation; it prescribes no evolution for $m$. None of these conclusions assumes a force law.

Let $m,c>0$, let $0<\delta<1$, and let $v\in\mathbb R^3$ have Euclidean norm satisfying $|v|/c\le\delta$. Put

$$z:=\frac{|v|^2}{c^2},\qquad \gamma:=(1-z)^{-1/2},\qquad p:=m\gamma v,\qquad E:=\gamma mc^2.$$

Then

$$0\le\gamma-1\le\frac{z}{2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},\qquad 0\le\gamma-1-\frac z2\le\frac{3z^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{5/2}},$$

and

$$|p-mv|\le\frac{m|v|^3}{2c^2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},\qquad 0\le E-mc^2-\frac12m|v|^2\le\frac{3m|v|^4}{8c^2(1-\delta^2)^{5/2}}.$$

If assigned SI kinematic units, $m$ is in kilograms, $c,v$ in metres per second, $p$ in kilogram metres per second and $E$ in joules. These are pointwise algebraic inequalities; they assume no equation of motion or empirical input.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, with vector-valued functions, their
components $f_i = \pi_i \circ f$, their limits and their continuity as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

1. **Continuity is componentwise.** Let $(X,d_X)$ be a metric space, $A \subseteq X$,
   $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and $a \in A$. Then $f$ is continuous at $a$ if and
   only if every component $f_i : A \to \mathbb{R}$ $(i<m)$ is continuous at $a$.
2. **Limits are componentwise.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit
   point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let
   $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. Then $\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$ if and only if
   $\lim_{x\to c} f_i(x) = L_i$ for every $i<m$ ([[def-function-limit]]).
3. **Algebra.** Let $(X,d_X)$, $A$, $a$ be as in clause 1, let
   $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous at $a$ and let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
   Then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ (defined pointwise) are continuous at $a$; the
   real-valued function $x \mapsto \langle f(x), g(x)\rangle$ is continuous at
   $a$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); and for every norm $N$ on
   $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ the real-valued function $x \mapsto N(f(x))$ is continuous at
   $a$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).

**Where $m \ge 1$ is spent.** The "if" direction of clauses 1 and 2 divides
$\varepsilon$ by $\iota(m)$, which requires $\iota(m) \ne 0$; and clause 3's last
part quotes a bound available only for $m \ge 1$. The "only if" directions hold
for every $m$ but say nothing at $m = 0$, there being no index $i < 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with

By [F2], $h(0)=0$ and $h'(s)=\frac12(1+s)^{-3/2}\le\frac12$ for $s\ge0$; if $u>0$, the mean value theorem gives $0\le h(u)\le u/2$, and for $u=0$ the same holds by equality. Hence, for every $(x,p)\in K$, $|V_c(p)-p/m|=(|p|/m)h(u)\le P_{\max}^3/(2m^3c^2)$. Expanding the component definition in [F3] gives $|a\times b|^2=|a|^2|b|^2-(a\cdot b)^2\le|a|^2|b|^2$, so $\|G_c(t,x,p)-G_N(t,x,p)\|_* = |V_c-p/m|/L_*+|q|\,|(V_c-p/m)\times\mathbf B(t,x)|/P_*\le\frac{P_{\max}^3}{2m^3c^2}\left(\frac1{L_*}+\frac{|q|B_{\max}}{P_*}\right)=C_*\epsilon_c$.

This proves the stated uniform field bound; stability will follow from the weighted-norm argument below.

Since $x_c$ is $C^2$, its speed stays strictly below $c$, and the mass-shell map is smooth, $p_c$ and $z_c$ are $C^1$; $z_N$ is $C^1$ by hypothesis. Let $H(s)=(H_x(s),H_p(s)):=G_c(s,z_c(s))-G_N(s,z_N(s))$, where each block is in $\mathbb R^3$. The same fields, mass, and charge are held fixed in the following formal family of model equations indexed by $c>0$; no Maxwell equations or empirical premise are added.

Choose reference scales $L_*>0$ metres and $P_*>0$ kilogram metres per second and define the dimensionless state norm

$$\|(x,p)\|_*:=\frac{|x|}{L_*}+\frac{|p|}{P_*}.$$

Let $K\subseteq\Omega\times\mathbb R^3$ be compact and convex, let $P_{\max}:=\sup_{(x,p)\in K}|p|$, $E_{\max}:=\sup_{(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\pi_xK}|\mathbf E(t,x)|$, and $B_{\max}:=\sup_{(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\pi_xK}|\mathbf B(t,x)|$. These field suprema are finite by the $C^1$ hypothesis on a compact cylinder. Set

$$B_*:=\frac{P_{\max}}{mL_*}+\frac{|q|}{P_*}\left(E_{\max}+\frac{P_{\max}B_{\max}}m\right).$$

For $c\ge P_{\max}/(m\delta)$, define the momentum-to-velocity map

$$V_c(p):=\frac{p}{m\sqrt{1+|p|^2/(m^2c^2)}}.$$

This is the velocity obtained from the massive mass shell and inverse momentum formula of [[pthm-rpm-inverse-momentum-and-work]]. Define the relativistic and Newtonian vector fields on $[0,T]\times K$ by

$$G_c(t,x,p):=\bigl(V_c(p),\,q[\mathbf E(t,x)+V_c(p)\times\mathbf B(t,x)]\bigr),\qquad G_N(t,x,p):=\bigl(p/m,\,q[\mathbf E(t,x)+(p/m)\times\mathbf B(t,x)]\bigr).$$

Suppose $G_N(t,\cdot)$ is Lipschitz on $K$ with constant $L\ge0$ in $\|\cdot\|_*$, where $L$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. For every $c$ in the family, $G_c$ and $G_N$ are bounded by $B_*$ in $\|\cdot\|_*$ on $[0,T]\times K$, since $|V_c(p)|\le P_{\max}/m$. For each $c\ge P_{\max}/(m\delta)$, let $J\subseteq I$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$ and let $x_c\in C^2(J,\Omega)$ satisfy $|\dot x_c(t)|<c$. $$C_*:=\frac{P_{\max}^3}{2m^3c_*^2}\left(\frac1{L_*}+\frac{|q|B_{\max}}{P_*}\right),$$

one has

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|(x_c(t),p_c(t))-(x_N(t),p_N(t))\|_*\le C_*\epsilon_c T e^{LT}.$$

Here $C_*$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Consequently the state difference is $O(c^{-2})$ on this fixed interval as $c\to\infty$, provided the common containment and Lipschitz hypotheses hold for the family.
